https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: The little-known friendship between Nina Simone and Langston Hughes
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
A new book charts how a 1949 meeting between the renowned poet and the legendary musician, then a 16-year-old girl, sparked enduring ties and fruitful collaboration

In 1949, the poet and writer Langston Hughes was already a towering figure – he toured the country reading his poems and lecturing, drawing crowds that filled auditoriums. That year, at a lecture in Asheville, North Carolina, Hughes met a 16-year-old girl, Eunice Waymon, who would go on to make history in her own right using her stage name, Nina Simone.

Hughes and Simone became friends and collaborators, working together on songs such as Backlash Blues, which soundtracked what was then a nascent Black Power movement. The song influenced Kwame Ture, the activist and Black revolutionary who was then known as Stokely Carmichael, who popularized the phrase “Black power”.

“Nina Simone refined the strategies of resistance Langston Hughes pioneered during the Harlem Renaissance to create the soundtrack to the civil rights movement and inaugurate the birth of Black Power,” writes W Jason Miller, author of Don’t Let Me Be Misunderstood: Nina Simone, Langston Hughes, and the Birth of Black Power, a new book that explores the previously underacknowledged relationship between Hughes and Simone.

Using new first-hand accounts and archives, Miller, a distinguished professor of English at North Carolina State University, writes a history of the friendship between two American heavyweights. The Guardian spoke to Miller about Langston Hughes, Nina Simone and their relationship.

How did you settle on writing about Langston Hughes and Nina Simone’s relationship?

I’ve been a Langston Hughes scholar for about 22 years. At a book event in Raleigh, I told the audience that Hughes was approached by a singer to write the liner notes for her album. And Langston Hughes’ response was, “Why, Nina, I’d be happy to.”

The audience gasped at the thought of their Nina Simone, North Carolina icon, being in connection with Langston Hughes. I knew immediately that I had to find out everything about these two. I found one single sentence that even mentioned Nina Simone in seven biographies about Hughes.

For the last six years, I tracked down every letter they exchanged, every time they were together and located one of Nina’s roommates, a woman who, at 91 years old, remembered the day that Langston Hughes came to their high school and first met Nina.

I don’t think that either Hughes or Simone receive as much credit as they should for their role in the Black Power movement. Can you talk a bit about that?

Langston Hughes is often introduced as a figure of the Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s, of which he was of course a leading figure. But Hughes died in May of 1967 – less than 11 months before Dr King’s assassination. He was active, involved and productive up until the very end.

In terms of Nina Simone, her oeuvre and her musical career were wide and far-reaching. When folks think about the civil rights movement and reduce it to nonviolence, they miss Nina’s key role. If Nina were a figure of the civil rights movement leadership, she’s more like [Kwame Ture] than she is like Malcolm X or Martin Luther King. She’s a fiery young figure that can get overlooked by people that don’t know, but the people that latch on to her know her iconic songs and her protest music. Their ability together created the soundtrack to the civil rights movement.

Langston Hughes really wanted to have a hit song written. He’d been trying since 1949 to break through in music. He had this desire to have Nina Simone sing one of his songs. The last poem that Hughes ever sent out for publication was called Backlash Blues. It’s the poem he gave to Nina to sing that became her iconic song.

This book is a biography of their friendship, which involves strategies for how two figures go through the practice of mentoring, building a relationship and collaborating. Nina sat in the third row at the 1960 Newport jazz festival while Hughes led a blues session in which he was directing Muddy Waters and John Lee Hooker for two and a half hours. Nina saw Hughes not just as an important cultural icon, she recognized him as a music lover that she could trust.

Leonard Bernstein and Walt Disney are generally more associated with making classical music accessible to a wider audience. But you argue that Simone did something similar with her interpolation of Bach in Love Me or Leave Me and a few other pieces.

Nina Simone grows up in Tryon, is educated in Asheville, North Carolina, with the goal of becoming a classical pianist. Her icon is Hazel Scott and her favorite musician of all time was Bach. What she was able to do in the very end of her career is combine popular music with classical music. She hides classical music inside of these popular songs. Unconsciously, audience members that listened to the vinyl or saw her in concert were being exposed to classical music.

For her first concert at Carnegie Hall, Andy Stroud, her manager husband, puts up a great deal of money, hires a big promoter, and they’re worried about being able to sell out. The first half of that entire concert is filled with classical instrumental music, not her singing. Langston Hughes had written promotional materials, so posters and newspaper ads had blurbs of support from Hughes.

What about their upbringing as southerners influenced their relationship and their wider reputations?

Nina Simone’s education in western North Carolina shapes her a great deal. She starts playing in the church. That area of the country gives us the incredible song Sinner Man, one she heard and performed. In late 1965, at the prompting of Langston Hughes, she records it, and it becomes a way to retell history. We’re not just thinking about God, the devil and the sinner. We’re thinking about student ambassadors who are trying to fight for change, white Klan members and the role of prayer in the civil rights movement.

Hughes’ grandmother spent time here in North Carolina with the Lumbee people. Right before he met Nina Simone, Langston Hughes gave a newspaper interview where he talked about his grandmother being part Lumbee and being part of the North Carolina tradition.

Hughes was condemned for his leftist politics and Simone faced similar condemnation. Do you think that their relationship informed their ability to use art to convey their political messages?

Langston Hughes not only recognized the talent that Nina Simone had, he not only had this desire to have his music performed, and he not only had a genuine interest in supporting the next generation, but he recognized that she could use the same strategies he had pioneered in the Harlem Renaissance. If you’re an academic, we call this signifying. If you’re a high school teacher, we call it allusion. But all people today know this as sampling.

Nina learned she could sample old music and update it. When she sang songs like Tomorrow Is My Turn, she turned a love song into a statement that tomorrow I’m going to get a chance. When she took songs like Go to Hell, Nina writes a new last verse. She says: we are in hell.

She brought this to her work in Sinner Man, especially. Nina activated those characters by thinking about Jimmy Lee Jackson and what started the march from Selma to Montgomery. When Nina used strategies to seem to be talking about something and slip it in, that’s when she was tuning her soul to the wavelength of Langston Hughes.

It starts with Langston Hughes’ spirit. The list of people he welcomed into his orbit and deliberately mentored is unbelievable. It includes Gwendolyn Brooks, Margaret Walker and he was very supportive of Amiri Baraka. I met a woman in Oxford, North Carolina – Mary “Pee Wee” Lindsay. She talked about meeting Hughes in the early 1950s, walking up to him with a couple pages of poems. She said that Hughes sat down with her for 30 minutes and went through those poems, even though she had no international-level talent, never published a book.

Simone and Hughes connected because, in so many ways, they were moving in the same direction. When Langston Hughes dies in 1967, Nina has Backlash Blues ready, but she hasn’t recorded or released it. After he dies, she writes a new verse. She includes their relationship. That leads her to understand one of Hughes’ key lessons, which is how to incorporate great people into music and art. One year later, she recognizes Martin Luther King’s assassination. Nina composed and thought of the song To Be Young, Gifted and Black in 1969. Hughes’ relationship sent her on this course of making music like Backlash Blues, Why the King of Love Is Dead, To Be Young, Gifted and Black that would stand as symbols of these great people.

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: ‘It was so satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen’: the people sick of being spied on by their smart TV
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
Is your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacy

Some may accuse Dan of being a luddite, but his master’s degree in computer science and decades of experience in telecommunications would suggest otherwise. “The tech is not intimidating,” he explains, “just increasingly enshittified.”

The first smart TVs entered the market in the late 2000s, when companies introduced operating systems, media players and apps to screens that were becoming wider and thinner. In recent years, the luxury status of smart TVs has waned and increasingly affordable options are widely available. Tom Parsons, TV and audiovisual editor at the electronics magazine What Hi-Fi?, explains that these cheaper models can struggle under more advanced features. “They’re not necessarily super-fast and responsive out of the box,” he says. “And then two, three, four years down the line, they can end up slowing down quite a lot under the weight of all that processing.”

Dan is just one of a growing number of tech-savvy watchers wishing their TVs weren’t so smart. Erin McQuiston and Matthew Schroyer, a couple from Connecticut, share his smart-screen scepticism.

“I don’t think we’ve ever used [our TV] as anything other than just a giant display,” says McQuiston. “There was a period where we were running it through an Xbox. And that was a constant battle because that was constantly being updated and patched and then you’d have to redownload all the apps for it.”

Meanwhile, Schroyer says his job as a software engineer has influenced his decision to “intentionally keep it very dumb” by keeping their TV disconnected from the internet. “A rule of the house is: don’t give things the wifi password,” he says. “It concerns me that folks increasingly have to be IT experts to get the bare minimum enjoyable experience out of this stuff.”

Instead, the 41-year-old connects his screen to an Apple TV box as a streaming workaround, and cites privacy as well as “highly invasive” advertisements for doing so. “Our living room is not a billboard for sale,” he says.

When asked how the couple might cope in a future where TVs may have mandatory internet, McQuiston says her husband is “handy enough to break every terms of service known to man and get in there and unsolder something to manually disconnect it”.

For Helen Northmore, a 51-year-old from Wales who works in AI delivery for the UK Health Security Agency, privacy is also a worry. Her grudge against smart screens began four years ago, when her faithful dumb TV broke without warning and she had to quickly find a replacement.

“We had already decided that we didn’t want the smart functionality, but it became really clear that it was very hard to find one that didn’t have any,” she says. Northmore, whose partner works in cybersecurity, says the couple wanted to “keep control” over their devices, which cost them a premium. “We were willing to pay more. One of the boundaries in how we live our lives is we want to minimise the smart element. We don’t have smart speakers. We don’t enable or connect to the internet.”

Today, she watches entertainment through a Sky box connected to her dumb TV, and dreads that when her current telly breaks there won’t be any option but to get a smart model and offer up her data.

More consumers are becoming worried about how their information is being used by manufacturers. “There are increasing privacy concerns around to what degree TVs are essentially scraping your data,” says Parsons. “TVs these days are full of sensors, including microphones, and that can make people nervous.”

But according to Parsons, despite interest in “dumber” models from some buyers, most shoppers want their TVs to be catch-all entertainment systems. The result is that the dumb TV market is almost nonexistent. “You can buy cheap monitors for signage,” he says, “but from a features point of view, you wouldn’t get the same performance that you would from a consumer TV.”

Paul, a public servant from Australia, knows just how hard finding a traditional TV can be. “When my last telly – a glorious 32-inch dumb TV – died recently, aged approximately 10 years old, I spent about three weeks scouring the city looking for something comparable. What I found is that they do not exist any more.”

After much searching, Paul discovered a single 40-inch TV without any smart functionality in the back of a shop. “It had zero ways to connect to the internet – just a couple of plugs on the back for making it work with the aerial on the roof and my VHS player, and that was it.” He remembers that it “was very dusty and cost about 200 dollars. Naturally, we fell instantly in love.”

“My friends all laugh at it when they come over,” he admits, “but secretly I know the joke is on them. My little telly doesn’t spy on me, and has a DVD player built in.”

The punchline may eventually land on Paul, however. In September, the Australian government launched a consultation into the future of the country’s free-to-air broadcasting, asking citizens for feedback on how TV should be accessed. One of the proposed scenarios would see traditional broadcast services cut in favour of streaming services and video on-demand apps.

In the same month, the UK government released a media green paper outlining its plan to fully move away from digital terrestrial television to services provided over a broadband connection by 2034 at the earliest. Such a situation would mean viewers having to rely on broadcaster apps and streaming services.

If a similar fate befell North America, James certainly wouldn’t care. He is originally from the US but now lives in British Columbia, Canada, and says traditional broadcast TV is “dead to him” and that he prefers to watch shows on streaming services or on YouTube. For the father and husband, privacy is a top priority.

“No one expects an end-user licence agreement to include giving up autonomy,” he says. “Having my TV listen to any conversation and use that for monetary or any form of gain is above and beyond expectations on the loss of privacy.”

In September, the YouTube channel Gamers Nexus released a two-hour investigation into LG Electronics’ smart televisions, saying that the devices record audio – even when they are offline or powered down. The South Korean company denied the allegations. In the fallout, some have taken measures to modify their smart TVs, regardless of brand or model. Some videos online show users replacing motherboards, cutting out Bluetooth and wifi modules and removing microphones from their TV remote controls.

Amid the controversy, James read online advice that modifying a TV remote microphone was a simple procedure. So he surgically removed the sensor himself. “Removing the mic was literally as easy as using a [craft] knife to scrape it off the top,” he says, “and the remote continued to work fine.”

James’s willingness to dissect his tech comes from fears for his children. “My kids are not teenagers and they have no agency to protect their private information,” he says. “Someone listening in on a TV gets to find out about my daughter’s first period without her knowing. And that is a level of invasion no one should have without explicit consent.”

Frustration and controversies have sparked a DIY interest in opening up and neutering the black rectangles in our living rooms. Though the desire in the first place may lead consumers to ask themselves an important question: have our TVs become too smart for their own good?

Gutting any piece of electronic equipment should be left to professionals. However, some may find that, for a complex problem, the simplest solutions are the most elegant. As Dan recalls: “It was enormously satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: Tom Cruise’s Digger is a commercial flop – but also the perfect climate film for our time
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
The movie follows Digger Rockwell, whose drilling triggers a vast iceberg that’s five times the size of Washington DC

Digger, the new Alejandro González Iñárritu film, is bombastic, misanthropic and an epic, critically savaged flop. It is also the near-perfect climate change film for our era.

Digger Rockwell, the eponymous protagonist played by Tom Cruise, is a bluntly caricatured Texas oilman blase about the environmental ruin of his drilling, even as it triggers a disastrous splitting of the Arctic ice sheet. This causes a vast iceberg, five times the size of Washington DC, to barrel towards Europe and threaten a devastating tsunami.

Much like this impending disaster and the real-world retreat of glaciers and coral reefs, though, the mere act of watching Digger has become a forlorn race against time. The box office failure has been resounding, and Digger’s time on the big screen has been brief.

Facing a predicted $245m loss – the lavishly made film took $8m in its first weekend in the US before dropping 60% for its second – Digger was yanked from more than 2,500 theatres across the US ahead of its third week. Scrambling to find a single cinema showing Digger, I had to resort to spending a Thursday lunchtime with just two other ticket-buying patrons at a major Manhattan venue.

The critical opprobrium and dismal ticket sales shouldn’t be a shock. Fans of Cruise are used to mass appeal movies of clean-cut heroism, not him aged, balding and dressed in a Stetson and cowboy boots and little else as he howls a confected Texan drawl in a dark climate satire.

The film also, as critics have pointed out, strays into a “glib and overblown” depiction of elite cowardice and cynicism when it comes to the climate crisis.

There are heavy-handed scenes of Digger eating endangered tuna in front of his aghast chief scientist Nirav Ganesh (a harried Riz Ahmed) and of sneering indifference from a US president (played dyspeptically by John Goodman) when confronted by the looming catastrophe.

“You know what, this isn’t my problem,” the president says when confronted with ecological and societal doom. A farcically bellicose, Pete Hegseth-like general dismisses the iceberg as a snow cone and advises the president to “blow that frozen cunt up” with nuclear weapons.

At one point, Digger and Ganesh sit in a room gazing at flickering flames, as if they are in hell. It’s not a cheery message, but it is a franker one than the other, scarce attempts to depict the climate crisis on screen. Perhaps we are actually in hell, the movie suggests, and the evil oil tycoons aren’t the only ones to blame for that.

It is cathartic to see Ganesh berate Digger for being guilty of the “most heinous act of all time” by knowing, as oil companies did in reality for decades, of the consequences of global heating but then fatally obscuring this knowledge in order to rake in more cash. But Digger goes further than just unmasking a single villain.

Don’t Look Up, the 2021 climate allegory, frames the problem as frantic scientists being ignored as an asteroid heads towards Earth. Digger’s message is a more sinister but uncomfortably accurate one – that we all know of the cataclysm we are inflicting upon current and future generations but have largely acquiesced to it.

“Let’s cut the bullshit, you love oil,” as Digger tells enraged European lawmakers, all dressed in muted beige and grey, in a lengthy rant. “You want to bask in your unsustainable lives.”

The oil companies may have lied and bought off politicians, but, in the wealthy west at least, we have all been complicit by failing to punish leaders for this and we remain willing customers for the poison of fossil fuels, even as they choke, drown and fry us.

Any sort of lifestyle change – eating less meat, flying less, switching to a car that doesn’t have a petrol pump on hand at each corner – is too much hassle for most of us even as we face the biggest threat to menace humanity. There are always, as Digger points out to the Eurocrats, phones to be charged, TikToks to watch. In holding up a mirror to this, Digger might not be the climate film we want. But it may be the one we need.

It’s striking that the possible end of a habitable planet has spawned comparatively little art with only vague nods, if at all, to our culpability. Among movies, there was Waterworld, another flop where Kevin Costner had to drink his own urine on a world flooded by the melted ice caps, and The Day After Tomorrow, where the melting ice causes a storm that plunges society into a new ice age.

Musically, the best of a meagre bunch is perhaps Smash Mouth’s 1999 hit song All Star which includes a lament of thinning ice and the line “my world’s on fire, how ‘bout yours?” The climate crisis may seem too overwhelming and gloomy to depict, but also, maybe we have so closeted and normalized our guilt that it feels shameful to bring it out into the light to be examined in public.

Digger forces us to not look away, even as we squirm at what we’ve done. “This film is a disaster movie,” Iñárritu has said. “But the disaster is us.”

The film is too nihilistic about our lack of response – Digger condemns clean energy as useless and his half-sister Emma (played by a squandered Sandra Hüller) makes endeavors in renewables that are dismissively mocked. Yet in real life the industry is growing explosively. We have everything we need to confront the climate crisis, after all, bar the necessary willpower.

Digger won’t be the last climate film. Later this year, A Statement, a dramatization of a real-life 1980 meeting of experts on what to do about global warming starring Paul Rudd and Paul Giamatti, will be released.

But Digger was the last Warner Bros’s theatrical release before it was purchased by Paramount Skydance and the Ellisons. Its commercial failure, along with the ideological leanings of the movie studio overlords, may deter further attempts to give us unvarnished tales of the climate crisis. That would be a huge, iceberg-sized mistake.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: DIY repair clubs are helping Americans save money and fight big tech
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
US community repair clinics teach people how to fix their belongings, pushing back against throwaway culture

On a recent Monday night, a volunteer-run workspace bustled with dozens of fixers in Brooklyn, New York. Some tinkered with sewing machines while others soldered circuit boards at a workbench. Caleb Young, a co-founder of the Brooklyn Spark space, fit a DIY suction device on to the handle of a Dyson vacuum cleaner.

“It’s in our culture to throw things away, but sometimes the fix is easier than you’d think,” Young said.

The Fixit Clinic is open every Monday night to walk-ins. Anyone with a broken item they’d like to fix – from torn clothes to malfunctioning electronic devices – can drop by during open hours and get the repair help and tools they need. It’s a way for people to push back against tech companies, making their phones and gadgets deliberately unrepairable so they buy newer devices while creating large amounts of e-waste. The clinics also foster community: once people learn to repair their possessions, many get addicted and like helping others, Young said.

“We like to tell them, ‘Why not take a few seconds to try and open something up?’” he said. “It’s broken anyway.”

The Brooklyn clinic is part of a nationwide network offering community repair. Peter Mui, who founded the first Fixit Clinic in Berkeley, California, in 2009, said that he has seen the number of clinics explode during the past few years; at least 2,000 have been hosted across the country. “We’re offering these workshops in libraries, at colleges and in public spaces where fixers and community members can come together,” Mui said.

Similar, unaffiliated clinics have seen success, too. The community-run Repair cafe, originally founded in Amsterdam, now has about 250 US locations. Neighborhood repair events at local community centers are also popping up around the country.

Policy proposals have even matched this grassroots demand. Since 2012, 24 states have successfully passed some form of right-to-repair legislation, mandating that manufacturers make their products repair-friendly instead of destined for the landfill. This year, 57 right-to-repair bills have been introduced in 22 states that would make machines such as phones, wheelchairs and construction equipment easier to repair. Members of Congress have also introduced a bipartisan federal automotive right-to-repair bill, called the Repair Act, but it has yet to be brought to a full House vote.

Mui attributes the growing interest to people questioning the environmental and economic costs of our consumer culture. “So much of our capitalist system is tied up in our endless consumption,” he said. “But if we come together to take agency and empowerment over the things we own, we can build a more sustainable future.”

The first modern right-to-repair state law was passed in 2012, when Massachusetts granted car owners the right to fix their cars at independent service shops. Congress passed a bill in 2014 that legalized “phone unlocking”, which allowed consumers to change their cell service carrier without buying a new phone. Farmers and states have also filed lawsuits against the agricultural equipment manufacturer John Deere over repair restrictions to their equipment, resulting in settlements with the company.

Right to repair reached a new level of public consciousness in 2024 when customers across the country were upset over broken McFlurry machines. The Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) protected the software on these machines, meaning only their manufacturer, Taylor, could fix them. After petitions from consumers and consumer advocacy groups, the US copyright office granted a copyright exemption that would allow third-party repairs on McFlurry machines.

Nathan Proctor, the senior director of the Right to Repair campaign at the Public Interest Research Group, said that corporations’ responses to right-to-repair laws have ranged from compliance to active resistance. For example, Apple has gradually made some parts and manuals available for repair, while the automotive industry has fought back against right-to-repair laws. “Some companies are hostile and refuse to provide repair materials, while others have made national policies to sell spare parts,” he said.

But the growing grassroots movement of community repair brings Proctor hope. “We need to both change the law and build out a culture of repair,” Proctor said. “To see these community events start up with no institutional backing – that’s a signal that something about repair is clicking with people.”

At San Jose State University in California, the Fixit Clinic student organization was recently voted the most influential club on campus. The student-led group holds monthly clinics for fellow students and community members at libraries around the city. “We like to tell people, ‘If you can get it through the door, we can fix it for you,’” said club president Lily Andrews.

Since the chapter was founded in 2024, the club has hosted on-campus and off-campus workshops to teach middle schoolers, college students and community members skills including sewing and soldering metals. Andrews, a college junior studying mechanical engineering, said that hosting these clinics has offered her hands-on practice that goes beyond the theories she is learning in the classroom. “When I open things up, I get to really see how they’re made, and see how the machinery components interact,” she said.

Andrews said she has learned how many of our products are made to discourage repair. “All these nuts, bolts and screws make it intimidating to take things apart,” she said.

Mui, the founder of the first Fixit Clinic, said that this is the next step in the clinics’ mission: launching more events in partnership with colleges and universities to educate the next generation of designers and engineers. “I’m focused on asking, ‘How do we train students to rethink the whole system?’” he said.

Andrews says that her experience leading the club has inspired her to pave a different path forward. “Fixing and repairing isn’t just an engineering skill; it’s a skill that everyone should have,” she said. “I want to keep applying what I’ve learned in my work so that we can keep items from landing in the landfill, help the environment and reduce waste.”

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: RJ Mitte obituary
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
Film and TV actor with cerebral palsy who played Walter White Jr in Breaking Bad and was a staunch disability rights campaigner

The actor RJ Mitte was a natural choice to play Walter White Jr, the son of Walter White (Bryan Cranston), the high school chemistry teacher turned meth dealer, in the television series Breaking Bad (2008-13), generally regarded as one of the greatest shows of the streaming era.

Walt Jr, also known as Flynn, was modelled by the show’s creator, Vince Gilligan, on the son of a friend who had cerebral palsy. Mitte had been diagnosed with cerebral palsy as an infant, and told the Guardian in 2015 that when he read the character summary he thought it “pretty much described me. ‘Dark hair, big eyebrows, cerebral palsy … ’ I was, like, ‘I have this covered.’”

He actually had to overplay the extent of his disability for the part (for example, depending on crutches that he did not need), and from the start his was a key role. Care for Flynn was part of the White family’s financial bind, but it was the boy’s changing relationship to his dad that became the audience’s window into Walt Sr’s progression into vicious gangster. Mitte grew alongside his character. “We watched him grow into a really fine actor ... that promise and potential now is a real loss,” said Cranston of his co-star.

His success as an actor helped Mitte, who has taken his own life aged 34, become a prominent activist for disabled people, working with the United Cerebral Palsy organisation and the Shriners Children’s hospital network. He did not believe cerebral palsy was a hindrance to him. “You develop a different look at how the world sees you and how you see the world,” he said. “I think it’s an asset.” And from early in his life he was determined to make it one.

I met RJ at the 2016 Paralympics Games in Rio, where I was a commentator for wheelchair basketball for the host broadcaster and he was working for the British TV station Channel 4. He was an amazing combination of intense focus and almost off-the-wall randomness, fuelled by incredible energy and, of course, a killer smile and laugh.

He was born, not breathing, via emergency caesarean section, in Jackson, Mississippi, and suffered brain damage during the delivery. Soon afterwards he was adopted by Dyna (nee Carriere) and RF Mitte Jr, and named Roy Frank Mitte III, later known as RJ (“Roy Junior”). Two months later, the couple split up, and Dyna raised her son alone. At three, RJ was diagnosed with cerebral palsy, and his legs were put in casts for six months, a process that would continue through his therapy in order to straighten his feet.

When RJ was 11, his younger sister, Lacianne (Lacey), was born, but a few weeks afterwards his mother was paralysed in a car accident. RJ helped financially by cutting lawns, doing odd jobs and collecting bottles for refunds.

He was as much father as brother to Lacey, who, in 2006, still an infant, was spotted in a Houston park by a talent scout who offered to represent her. The family moved to Los Angeles, where her agency also arranged acting lessons for RJ. He got small parts in Everyone Hates Chris and in Hannah Montana, before being hired for Breaking Bad, which debuted in January 2008, when he was 15. It ran for five seasons and won six Emmy awards, including in 2014 the prize for best ensemble cast.

In 2013, Mitte won the Screen Actors Guild’s Harold Russell award, given in recognition of those “who advance the accurate portrayal and employment of people with disabilities”. “Hollywood has always portrayed disability as a weakness, something you have to overcome,” Mitte said. “To me it’s the complete opposite ... it’s a personal challenge to grow and explore.”

After Breaking Bad, Mitte appeared on TV in an episode of Vegas (2013) and then a full season in Switched at Birth (2014), as a wheelchair user, the love interest for the deaf girl Daphne, one of the “switched” characters of the title.

His film work was largely with independents, in a number of horror and crime films, and others where his cerebral palsy was a part of the story. Who’s Driving Doug (2016) is a road movie written by a man with muscular dystrophy. Mitte was particularly good in the Australian Standing Up for Sunny (2019), in which he played a disabled man who is dragged into an attempt to make a hesitant standup comic more confident. Critics praised the comic timing between Mitte and Philippa Northeast, as the comedienne.

In Triumph (2021), Mitte played a bullied student with cerebral palsy who takes up wrestling to prove himself in high school. On TV he played the Mind Master in 2022 in the successful part-animated series The Guardians of Justice. Perhaps his most impressive film was the poorly distributed All the Little Things We Kill (2019), in which a college professor holds a classroom hostage in order to get a ban on semi-automatic weapons passed.

Earlier this year, in the film Talking to Strangers, he played a loner with cerebral palsy who opens his tightly structured world to an exuberant woman, who later tells him that she plans to take her own life. One Eye Open was scheduled for release in the week of Mitte’s death; another film, Cassi, has been finished and awaits its release date.

In 2025, Mitte announced his engagement to his long-term girlfriend Kennedy Suarez. He is survived by his mother and sister.

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: Canadian Smarties, honeycomb bars and 12 international candies way better than Snickers
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
Forget the familiar favorites and try these sweets from around the world – from caffeine-boosted chocolate drops to dragonfruit gummies – available before Halloween

Welcome to Filter finds, a series where Guardian staff and Filter contributors share the things we love most – and think you might, too.

Every October, we set out to rot our teeth on the same high fructose corn-syrup candies. Twizzlers! Snickers! Almond Joy! But these words have no meaning outside of the US. Beyond the hegemony of Hershey, Mars and Mondelēz lies a world of honeycomb bars, caffeine-boosted chocolate drops and dragonfruit gummies that the American mind simply can’t comprehend … though maybe our stomachs can.

We asked our Guardian colleagues for their favorite candy from around the world – be they childhood treats or souvenirs picked up through travels abroad – that we don’t need a plane ticket to try ourselves. They’re all available online, and yes, we checked: as of publication, they will all arrive before Halloween.

This is Italian chocolate with real espresso in the center, making it both a sweet treat and a caffeine boost. Italian markets tend to stock it during winter, and it can be hard to track down outside those months. It’s a unique candy and a souvenir I always try to bring back from Italy, as it’s not always available and hasn’t been introduced in the US like other Ferrero candy products (such as Nutella, Kinder, Ferrero Rocher and Tic Tacs). Michael Sainato, Guardian US labor reporter

It’s a nutty toffee that tastes a little more toasty (dare I say almost burnt?) than American counterparts. It may crack your teeth, and the choice to put a rodent mascot on a food wrapper may be questioned by some. But the texture and the vintage packaging are all part of the charm. Tea time is a fixture in Russian homes, and this sweet was always on offer in our family when I was growing up in the 90s. Today, I buy it on Brighton Beach, and I’m glad to see it available online. Childhood memories are fallible, but I think it tastes just the way it used to. Ivan Kuraev, engineer

Growing up in Abu Dhabi, these hard Thai Heartbeat candies were everywhere. We would find them at school, in the candy bowls our teachers kept in the classroom as well as in supermarkets and baqalas – our local corner stores. After spending recess running around in the Abu Dhabi heat, getting handed one before heading back into the freezing air-conditioning was always a real treat. I love the lychee flavor most, but strawberry and orange are just as fruity, sweet and tangy. My friends and I would sneak a few extras from the bowl into our uniform pockets when our teachers weren’t looking – only every now and then, of course! Maya Yang, breaking news reporter and live blogger

These Lebanese chocolates are simply the best chocolates in the world – and a core part of a childhood spent in the Gulf. Their gold- and silver-wrapped chocolates seemed to be in every home, brought out when guests came over, and at weddings, baby showers and other celebrations. My friends and I always went for the milk chocolate squares, especially the ones filled with wafers or hazelnuts. Plenty of chocolate shops have come and gone across the UAE, but Patchi has stayed a constant. For many of us who continue to grapple with our third-culture kid identities, a Patchi chocolate is a comforting link to our Gulf childhoods – a reminder that despite constant change, some things stay the same. Yang

Alfajores are a little piece of Argentinian heaven. They are pillowy soft cookies with luscious dulce de leche in the middle and covered in dark chocolate. What makes them especially fun is how varied they are: different regions and provinces have versions with different cookies, fillings, coatings and textures. You might find the classic dulce de leche-filled alfajor from Buenos Aires, or regional favorites including the alfajores from Córdoba or Mar del Plata, which come with quince jam and are covered in white powdered sugar. Some are soft and crumbly, others are cakier and spongy. They’re the kind of candy that makes every trip through Argentina a chance to discover a new favorite. Ana Cutello-Edgar, senior manager of editorial operations

This chocolate-covered honeycomb bar from the UK has a light, crispy texture that shatters as you bite into it and then melts in your mouth. I love the contrast between the smooth chocolate and the crunchy honeycomb, and there’s something wonderfully nostalgic about it. It’s also the kind of candy that feels distinctly British to me, which makes it exciting to seek out when I’m missing a trip or craving something I can’t easily find at the grocery store. I make a special trip to McLean Avenue in Yonkers, where there’s a heavy concentration of all things British. It’s sweet, a little messy, incredibly satisfying and totally worth the visit to that part of New York. Cutello-Edgar

Rare is the candy that can sneak chia seeds in and not tarnish the appeal. Hi Chews are a staple of my pantry – a taffy-like texture that doesn’t coat or risk breaking my teeth, and consistently strong flavors that resemble real fruit better than most gummies. Hailing from Japan, Hi Chews are increasingly prominent in the US and boast a wide variety of flavors to keep your taste buds guessing. The Superfruit pack is a personal favorite, differing from the more traditional “tropical fruit” options in the candy aisle, with the kiwi and açai especially tasty. Jeff Rueter, soccer correspondent

You and I probably have very different ideas of Smarties. Whereas your Smarties might make your nose crinkle a bit at their fruity tartness, mine make me think of the perfect chocolate topping for a sundae (bonus points if it’s TCBY frozen yogurt, a brand that had us collectively losing our minds when it came to Canada in the late 80s). Canadian Smarties are best characterized as flatter and wider M&Ms, with a creamier and softer chocolate interior offset by a satisfying crunchy candy shell. As kids, we used to trade Smarties colors at recess with the enthusiasm of Pokémon cards, and to this day, getting a blue one ignites that same thrill. They’re delightful one by one but even better by the handful. Marissa Miller, Filter US contributor

I wasn’t like other kids on Halloween: I wasn’t pining for the lollipops, the gummy bears nor the Sour Patch Kids. Even before my parents allowed me to ever take baby sips from their morning espresso, I was holding out my pumpkin-shaped bag with high hopes for a Coffee Crisp (jackpot for a full-sized bar). An iconic Canadian treat, it gets its airy yet satisfying bite from coffee-flavored cream sandwiched between light vanilla wafer cookies. The whole bar is enrobed in milk chocolate that melts so instantly it barely requires chewing. While it is by no means a premium chocolate bar, nor particularly hard to find in stores, it’s worth popping into your carry-on if Canada is ever on your bucket list. Miller

Is there anything better than a grocery store in a country where you don’t live? The produce, the packaging and – crucially – the Haribo. Even the varieties you can get in the States are better abroad (give me a Schtroumpf over a Smurf any day), but France’s Orangina Pik is undefeated. It’s the gummy sour candy form of an afternoon at a brasserie; you might be choking on an old man’s secondhand smoke, but you’re sipping the most refreshing beverage of your life – worth the airfare to Paris but mercifully available online. Ruth Baron, senior editor, US newsletters

I first tried these as a teenager during my family’s big trip to Italy when I was 14, and I was instantly hooked – I ate them by the dozen. Since then, I’ve located every store near my parents’ house on Long Island and my New York City apartment that sells them in case I need an emergency bar or two. (I’m devastated to say I also eat them in smaller quantities less frequently now.) With milk chocolate, a crispy wafer and creamy hazelnut filling, these bars have everything you could want in a candy (unless you’re allergic to hazelnuts – in which case, I’m so sorry for your loss). My husband argues that Ritter Sport is better, but he’s wrong and what is marriage if not a union where you can agree to disagree? Anyway, someone needs to create a cake version of a Bueno bar because I’d probably never have another birthday cake! Jenna Amatulli, Guardian US deputy head of news

These milky and chewy candies are a childhood staple for generations of Chinese kids, from Lunar New Year celebrations to everyday snacks shared with friends on the playground. The candy is wrapped in edible sticky rice paper, which melts immediately in your mouth and leaves with the sweet, creamy and nostalgic aftertaste of the candy. Hazel Tang, video producer

In every new country, one of my must-see attractions is the local grocery store. I love knowing the in-season produce, the potato chip variety and, as a vegan, if there are new and interesting snacks free of animal products. To my enormous surprise, I found an entire wall of Treets in a local supermarket in the small-ish city of Dortmund, Germany. My favorites were Crispy (chocolate-coated puffed rice) and Peanuts, which is essentially a Peanut M&M but better, since it’s cruelty-free. The company gets bonus points for paper packaging, even if that means you need to snack quickly for peak freshness (oh, the horror!).

(And as a Canadian, it’s my patriotic responsibility to endorse the Crispy Crunch, a chocolate and peanut butter bar. Americans might recognize the flavor profiles from Butterfinger: it’s crispy, it’s flaky, it’s filled with peanut butter – something we first patented. The second a vegan version rolls out, I will buy a thousand.) Jessie Willms, SEO strategist

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Trump’s obsession with Ilhan Omar has reached a dangerous new level | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The administration seems intent on stripping the congresswoman of her US citizenship and deporting her. It’s a terrible abuse of power

What do you think it is about Ilhan Omar, exactly, that seems to get under Donald Trump’s tangerine-tinted skin? The president has claimed he has a problem with the progressive Democratic congresswoman because she is “unpatriotic” to the US and “disrespectful … to Israel”. However, the extent of his animus towards Omar, the first Somali American in Congress, suggests there’s more to it. Trump has insisted he is “the least racist person there is anywhere in the world”, so I’m sure it has nothing to do with the fact that she’s brown and Muslim. Truly, it’s a mystery.

Whatever the reason, Trump’s not a fan. The president has plenty of enemies, but few have been attacked as ferociously and consistently over the years as Omar. He’s called her “garbage”, among other nasty names, suggested (without evidence) that she married her brother, and said she “should be thrown the hell out of our country”. His supporters have echoed his calls to deport Omar, who fled war-torn Somalia as a child and became a naturalised US citizen at 17.

Now Trump’s obsession with Omar has reached a dangerous new level. Trump isn’t just throwing out insults any more; his administration seems intent on stripping the congresswoman of her US citizenship and deporting her. Last Monday, 22 days before the November midterms in which Omar is seeking re-election, federal agents raided her house in Washington DC. Her phone was seized and grand jury subpoenas were reportedly issued to some of her relatives as part of an investigation concerning her immigration paperwork. Trump, by the way, denied any involvement. Just a curious coincidence that one of his biggest nemeses is now being treated like a criminal.

As House Democratic leaders have said, the raid on Omar’s house “raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponisation of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries”. But it also raises another question: is this “just” a stunt designed to embarrass and intimidate Omar before the midterms? Or is there a real possibility that the congresswoman could be denaturalised and deported?

“Certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen,” Tom Homan, Trump’s “border czar”, told Fox News over the weekend when asked about Omar being deported. “We’ll let the evidence lead where it leads, but she’ll be held to the same standard you and I are held: if she violated the law, then she’ll be held accountable,” Homan added.

Oh, please. I know the Mar-a-Lago set are big on Botox, but I can’t believe Homan was able to preach about accountability with a straight face. Not many people are convicted of 34 felonies and face no jail time. Trump, however, is in the White House rather than prison because the supreme court’s conservative majority (which he helped create) found that former presidents are entitled to a degree of immunity from criminal prosecution.

The US government has every right to uphold its immigration laws, but its appetite seems to vary considerably depending on the person. If Homan really is so keen on accountability, may I suggest he take a look at the Trump megadonor Elon Musk? The tech mogul’s brother, Kimbal Musk, has publicly joked about the fact that the brothers briefly worked in the US without proper documentation in the 1990s. (Elon said it was a “grey area”.) And then there’s Melania Trump: in 2016, the Associated Press reported the first lady was paid for 10 modelling jobs in the US before she had legal permission to work in the country. (Melania has denied ever violating the terms of her immigration status.)

Omar was just a teenager when her father filled out the paperwork that led to them both being naturalised. I obviously have no idea if there were any errors in that. But I can tell you that this “investigation” is not about accountability. It is a terrifying abuse of power that reflects the way in which the Trump administration is weaponising the immigration system to stamp out dissent. We’ve already seen Trump deport noncitizen student activists to crack down on pro-Palestinian speech. Now he’s applying that strategy to Omar, a sitting congresswoman. As Barack Obama warned at the weekend, “If this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her.” Indeed it won’t; Trump is just getting started.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: We can stop Trump’s assault on the international criminal court | Kenneth Roth
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Many applauded when Navi Pillay was awarded the Nobel peace prize. The South African human rights lawyer had chaired the UN commission of inquiry that found Israel to have committed genocide in Gaza and served for five years as a judge on the international criminal court (ICC).

Donald Trump responded a few hours later by imposing sanctions on the ICC. He chose a moment for celebrating the rule of law to try to undermine it.

Trump had already sanctioned 13 ICC judges and prosecutors, obstructing their access to credit cards, bank accounts and the modern economy. The new sanctions target the entire institution. If they take effect in six months as threatened, they would effectively bar all financial transactions with the court – and more.

They would starve it of cash; no banks would be able to do business with it. They could force internet companies to halt the court’s email and computer systems and telecom companies to cut its phones. And they would preclude human rights groups and victims from working with the court. Violators would risk penalties themselves.

The sanctions are the latest step in Trump’s effort to make the world safe for American and Israeli war criminals. He wants the ICC to agree, presumably during the six-month hiatus, never to prosecute the national of a country that has not joined the court, even when the individual commits a crime on the territory of a member state.

This is a battle that the US government fought and lost when the court’s founding treaty was adopted in Rome in 1998. The US position was repudiated overwhelmingly, with the treaty approved by a vote of 120 to 7.

In justifying the latest sanctions in the name of American sovereignty, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, conjured up images of the ICC prosecuting Trump officials as they detain migrants. That is scaremongering. The court has no jurisdiction over crimes committed inside the United States and never claimed it.

But other countries have a sovereign right to prosecute crimes committed on their territory, even if the perpetrator is an American or an Israeli. Ordinarily that would be done by a country’s regular courts, but if in extreme circumstances those courts were unwilling or unavailable, governments have a sovereign right to delegate that power to the ICC. That’s what joining the ICC entails.

The Trump-Rubio view is that the US and Israel have a sovereign right to commit war crimes wherever they want, and no other government has a sovereign right to have them prosecuted. That is laughable.

Fortunately, other governments see through the Trump-Rubio sophistry. Only Venezuela, which since Trump’s capture of former president Nicolás Maduro has become a US vassal state, and Chad, which receives significant US military aid, have heeded Washington’s call and announced plans to withdraw from the court. (Three Russian-backed military juntas in the Sahel have also announced an intention to withdraw for their own self-protective reasons.) Even if they all follow through, that would leave a solid 120 governments fully onboard.

The most important step would be for the European Union to invoke its “blocking statute”, which, when activated, prohibits European companies from complying with US sanctions outside US territory. European banks would have to continue providing services to the court. So would telecom, internet and other European companies.

The EU has already invoked the blocking statute in two prior circumstances – to limit US sanctions against Cuba and Iran. Trump’s threat to destroy one of the world’s foremost institutions of justice is a very appropriate third case.

Why hasn’t the EU already done so? One significant obstacle seems to be Dutch banks. The ICC is located in The Hague. If Dutch banks were ordered under the blocking statute to ignore Trump’s sanctions, they might face retaliation.

But Europe has tools to fight back. When Trump rattled on about seizing Greenland, European leaders responded by threatening to deploy their economic “bazooka” – officially known as the Anti-Coercion Instrument – which would restrict designated American companies from operating in Europe. Trump backed down.

The ICC also has an important tool in its arsenal. Article 70 of its founding Rome Statute makes it a crime (with a potential prison sentence of up to five years) to obstruct justice by intimidating or retaliating against court personnel for their official duties.

That’s what Trump’s and Rubio’s sanctions do. The ICC president, Judge Tomoko Akane of Japan, said as much in responding to them.

They were imposed because court personnel charged the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the former Israeli defense minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes in Gaza and opened an investigation that might have included torture by US personnel under the George W Bush administration.

The court had jurisdiction even though neither the United States nor Israel has joined the court because these alleged crimes took place on the territory of the member states Palestine and Afghanistan.

Trump and Rubio might try to laugh off being charged by the ICC, but their world would become much smaller. They would suddenly risk arrest if they traveled to any ICC member state. They should ask the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, facing his own ICC arrest warrant, how he felt being unable to travel to the Brics summits in South Africa and Brazil. Trump’s pardon power does not extend to the ICC.

Charging a US president or secretary of state would obviously be a big deal. It would take a courageous chief prosecutor to take the step. Unfortunately, the ICC currently has no chief prosecutor since Karim Khan was ousted for sexual misconduct.

Two deputies, Nazhat Shameem Khan and Mame Mandiaye Niang, are serving as interim leaders. While the ICC is under attack, its member states are inexplicably dawdling in naming a successor. Urgent action is required.

Meanwhile, all of us should make clear what Trump’s sanctions are really about. The ICC is far from perfect, but it has done important work on behalf of the victims of mass atrocities in Ukraine, Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Myanmar, Afghanistan, the Philippines and elsewhere.

Trump would sacrifice all of that for his lawless views on American and Israeli crimes. Supporters of selective justice might endorse his quest for impunity. No one else should.

Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Kenneth Roth

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment

Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal.

That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI.

People expect AI to lead to fewer jobs in 34 of the 37 countries surveyed by the Pew Research Center. In wealthy countries like the US, Australia and South Korea, about seven in 10 expect job losses over the next 20 years. And across countries, concern among young people is rising. While fears focus on job numbers, the bigger change will be what jobs become.

The nature of human work will move towards judgment. Experts refer to AI as “jagged”, superhuman at certain tasks but weak at others, with no clear boundary between the two. AI rapidly improves where work can be automatically checked and examples are endless. But it’s shaky where no automated test can determine whether the answer is right. Even if AI is correct a majority of the time on a task, it often doesn’t tell you when it’s inaccurate. If you’ve used AI, you’ve probably experienced how it can be confidently wrong.

Some of these errors will solve themselves as models get better. But jaggedness is a symptom of how these models learn. I see this often as a technology leader building with these systems.

A smarter model still needs a right answer to learn from. When one gap is closed, it shows up somewhere else no one thought to check. But many business decisions don’t immediately have a clear right answer. Whether a choice is good depends on a future no one can see and data no one has. That’s where judgment comes in. So AI will keep mastering tasks that have checkable results but struggle where a person has to decide what a good outcome looks like.

As a result, a new type of work is starting to appear. Someone tests whether the output of AI is correct based on real work, not just on benchmarks. Someone sets limits on what AI is allowed to do before it runs, so the worst mistakes are avoided. Someone runs and manages several agents the way a shift manager runs a crew. Picture an airport control tower. Radar and software track flight paths, with humans judging the few that matter to avoid collisions. No one is manually watching every screen. That would never scale.

Setting AI’s limits is harder than it sounds. In a 2026 study, after an agent was told to protect a secret, it destroyed its own email server, deleting every single email. It was given a goal, without any limits on what it could do. The researchers described it as the right values paired with terrible judgment. Deciding what is off limits and what a mistake would cost takes someone who knows the work and will answer for the result.

Here is the good news for people worried about their own jobs. The people best suited for doing this new type of work aren’t computer programmers. They are the ones who know how the real work is done. Catching what a confident AI left out or got wrong takes someone who knows the complete answer. That knowledge is uncheckable, unwritten and takes the form of judgment honed over years of doing the task and watching it break.

Ford recently learned the value of human expertise. In recent years, it leaned hard on automating its quality control, cutting thousands of jobs. But earlier this year, it had to rehire 350 veteran engineers to oversee the process and hunt for failure points before a part reached the factory floor. They brought the judgment of watching parts fail over years. With humans at the helm, Ford’s quality ranking then hit first among mainstream brands for the first time since 2010.

But we are making a serious mistake with the jobs we’re eliminating due to AI: the entry-level, routine ones. That routine work is how judgment gets built over time. Junior employees work under the supervision of senior experts until their experience turns into instinct. AI eliminates the friction related to learning how to do the job. But the demand for judgment did not go away. We are just destroying the path to developing it.

The real question is not whether machines will take over our work. It is whether we will have the people who can tell when the machines are wrong. Right now, we are automating the training ground where judgment is learned. If you have hard-earned expertise about anything, the next few years will only make you more valuable. And if you are just starting out, the old apprenticeship model will not hand it to you. You have to go and earn it, deliberately, on tasks the machines cannot yet judge.

Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Jalen Hurts played through a blood clot. Are NFL players cattle?
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The Eagles quarterback’s recent health issues highlight how football’s toughness culture puts its players at risk

Jalen Hurts is likely to miss the rest of the NFL season after an ultrasound revealed blood clots in his lungs. Thankfully, he’s now restricted from playing for the immediate future, meaning he won’t be risking serious complications – or even his life – as he did when he played in the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 5 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars in London.

The quarterback complained to the Eagles’ medical staff of calf pain on 8 October, according to ESPN. The Eagles say Hurts flew to London with the rest of the team and, out of an “abundance of caution”, was given an ultrasound. The test found a superficial clot in his calf. Doing an ultrasound before the flight would’ve been the most prudent thing. The same for making him inactive after the clot was found. But instead, he played in the game on 11 October, as the medical staff and doctors in London agreed “that activity and mobility were important”. Hurts also practiced all last week before a follow-up ultrasound also found clots in his lungs.

Some have celebrated Hurts’s performance against the Jaguars as a feat of virility; to many it looks more like putting a player in real danger. His blood clots could have caused serious health issues during the flights or game. (One sports medicine doctor told NJ.com that Hurts was “a walking risk”.) If his condition was dire enough that doctors reportedly told him in the early hours of Sunday morning not to sleep before the Jaguars game, he shouldn’t have been playing. Hurts’s agent, Nicole Lynn, clarified that he did get some sleep before facing the Jaguars, but the question remains: was the NFL’s London showcase so important that it was worth risking Hurts’s life?

Asked about his decision to play Hurts, Eagles coach Nick Sirianni told reporters that he relies on advice from medical staff. “I’m a football coach. I lean on our medical experts in every situation,” he said. “I have full trust and full faith in them. It’s not just me that has major care for our players. It’s them as well.”

The Super Bowl LIX MVP is on blood thinners and hopefully on the road to healing, expected to make a full recovery. But his ordeal is the latest example of how football players are put in danger season after season. One piece of research from 2017 found that a college player took hits to his head during a single game that were equivalent to multiple car crashes. A study published this year found that 215 of 235 brains of former NFL players donated for research showed signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease that can only be diagnosed after death. The NFL has said that it “continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing ⁠strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts” but players keep on suffering concussions, and others like Hurts find themselves in a football culture where playing through injury is commonplace.

Last Wednesday, Hurts told reporters that his last week had been a “very unique experience” but declined to reveal the blood clot. No one has reported that he received any undue pressure from the Eagles or the league to play against the Jaguars. But it wouldn’t be shocking; this isn’t even the Eagles’ first controversial injury in London. In 2018, former Eagles tackle Lane Johnson was reportedly “berated” by general manager Howie Roseman for saying he was unsure about playing because of a high ankle sprain. After suiting up, Roseman reportedly told him, “Good, you have your mouthpiece in, now you can’t say anything stupid.” Neither man has commented on the matter, but it appears to offer a glimpse of life in the good ol’ NFL, where admitting you’re impaired is stupidity. Johnson aggravated the ankle injury and suffered a knee injury during the game.

Football culture demands players “tough it out” and get on the field. As former NFL receiver Bernard Berrian has said, the tension “isn’t verbal” but is still “there” because, “as we say, you can’t make the team in the training room.” Former running back Clinton Portis echoed Berrian when he spoke about playing through 10 concussions in his career and rarely getting treatment: “You can’t make the club in the tub.” Portis said he was “really scared” of undergoing testing to assess his neurological health.

You can see how the culture of the NFL makes players behave this way. With only 61% of NFL contracts containing guarantees, and an average 56% year-to-year retention, the pressure to stay active and keep the checks coming in is rampant. Pretty much every job pressures its employees to perform in some capacity; only one entails 300lb men running full speed to tackle you for 17 games a season. Players shouldn’t be made to feel they need to be on the field, but the irrational “win now” pressure they face trickles down and paints them in two colors: as an asset or expendable. It’s inherently inhumane.

The NFL has attempted to address injuries, and the threat of concussion and CTE in particular, but those efforts don’t seem to be enough. The league has changed kickoff rules and introduced oversized Guardian Caps to mitigate concussions, but football’s physical risks persist. A 2018 study in the Brain Neurology Journal revealed that subconcussive hits also contribute to CTE. And a 2025 Wisconsin School of Medicine study concluded that Guardian Caps did not reduce concussion rates in a sample of high school players. It’s unclear what seismic changes could actually address football’s inherent brutality. And the NFL’s struggles to stop it shows it is unsure – or doesn’t care enough – too.

Hurts’s case also raises the specter of medical racism. Multiple studies have shown that Black people and other minorities in the United States are less likely to receive adequate medical care than white people. It’s impossible to say whether the staff who treated Hurts looked at a strapping Black athlete and believed he could play a brutal game while suffering from blood clots. But the incident nonetheless conjures historical patterns and lived experiences of Black people not receiving proper care.

Hopefully Hurts gets back on the field and has a long, healthy career. Regardless, the Eagles’ handling of his treatment should be a demarcation point for the league. From the top down, the NFL needs to stop treating its labor force like cattle on a farm, as if their sole worth is in putting their bodies at risk.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on Alberta’s referendum: Canada holds together – against Donald Trump | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Voters’ emphatic rejection of separation strengthens Mark Carney’s energy strategy in the face of a US trade war and threats

Canadians are proving to be a voice of sanity. In roundly rejecting the idea of separating from Canada, voters in the oil- and gas-rich province of Alberta sensibly backed the nation-building strategy of the prime minister, Mark Carney. He has put Alberta at the centre of his plan to make Canada an energy superpower that is “much less dependent on the United States”.

Donald Trump’s trade war and threats last week to make Canada the 51st US state were a fillip for Mr Carney in Alberta, a landlocked western province where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular. The stakes were high: a successful separatist campaign would have handed Mr Trump leverage over Canada’s resource belt. The result instead lets Mr Carney cast Alberta’s mineral wealth as a national asset, rather than allow separatists to define it as a regional grievance.

Albertans were not offered a binding secession vote. They rejected the idea of beginning the process towards such a vote. The early result – roughly 75% against 25% – looks emphatic. For all the separatists’ talk of “success”, Albertans did not buy their tactical argument: that voting for a future referendum would strengthen the province’s hand against Ottawa. However, the sense of alienation in the province is profound: polls show that Albertans think most of the country does not respect the region.

Addressing that alienation has come at a worrying cost, both politically and environmentally. Mr Carney, who was raised in Alberta’s capital, Edmonton, made a series of pacts with the province’s premier, Danielle Smith. He agreed to back a new 1m-barrel-a-day oil pipeline and tear up environmental rules. Mr Carney has to deliver tangible gains, or else the sizable faction that supports separatism within Ms Smith’s United Conservative party will entrench itself and look for future opportunities to act.

Whatever replaces the “Let Alberta decide” movement will have an uphill struggle. In his book The Republic of Alberta, the journalist Tyler Dawson wrote that it has “no charismatic leader like René Lévesque, the suave, smoke-wreathed Quebec separatist who took his province to its 1980 secession referendum. There is no culturally entrenched canon of nationalist literature to fill Alberta bookshelves. The province has no unique language or race or faith that binds its residents together.” Yet victory this month for the Lévesque-founded Parti Québécois in provincial elections reveals that separatists can win power despite their raison d’etre being unpopular.

To those who witnessed the Brexit referendum, the Albertan poll offered a depressing rerun of nationalist gripes and political fantasy. The easy assurance that sovereignty can be recovered painlessly is wearily familiar. Keith Wilson, an architect of Alberta’s separatist movement, calling the task of founding a country “super easy” will prompt a sense of deja vu. Perhaps most importantly, Blackfoot leaders saying that separatists regarded treaty nations as a “speed bump” is a sign that the sovereigntists have not caught up with the fact that First Nations’ rights are belatedly being recognised as a critical part of Canada’s constitutional makeup.

Canada’s unity is a political achievement that is continually negotiated among regional interests, Québécois nationhood, Indigenous people’s rights, new arrivals and the continental pull of the US. Paradoxically, the insecurity that characterises Canadians keeps them in check – and holds the nation together. Or as one of the country’s most famous novelists put it: Canada is “not a country you love, it is a country you worry about”.
