https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: James Talarico Is Preaching a Gospel of Pluralism
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
It’s a question one Senate hopeful has repeatedly asked on the campaign trail. To anyone who’s followed the last 40 years of American politics, this merging of preaching and politics may not sound particularly novel. But the candidate’s answer—and his party affiliation—marks a surprising departure from the usual partisan scripts.

“I think he would tell the senators on the floor, ‘Depart from me,’” James Talarico has told audiences. “For I was hungry and you cut my food assistance. I was sick and you kicked me off Medicaid. I was a stranger and you deported me and my family.”

Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian, is running on a compassionate, liberal Christianity rarely seen since the right gained a stranglehold on faith-forward politics decades ago. But in recent years, Republicans, previously the bastions of good old-fashioned, Focus on the Family traditionalism, have rolled over to the dark underbelly of their movement. Exit: modest family values. Enter: barstool conservatism.

In doing so, they’ve created an opening for Democrats who make their religious convictions central to their politics. And unlike the Moral Majority of years past, these liberal candidates are preaching a faith that’s inclusive, optimistic, and winning support on both sides of the aisle.

Entrenched though it’s been, the “God gap” between Democrats and Republicans is a relatively recent creation. The Republican Party platform from 1972 contains no references to God, and in 1976, evangelicals voted for the Sunday-school teachings of Jimmy Carter.

That all changed in the 1980s with Reagan’s embrace of Jerry Falwell, who urged his fellow evangelical pastors to bring politics to the pulpit and push their congregations toward conservative candidates. The conflation of Republican beliefs and Christian identity had officially begun, and after decades of work from the likes of Pat Robertson, James Dobson—culminating in eight years of President George W. Bush—there was no stopping the merger.

But just when the God gap had reached its peak, Trump slithered in. While his extramarital affairs and long history of alleged sexual misconduct always made for an uneasy allegiance with the religious right, the president has more recently drawn fire from Christian groups for posting an AI image depicting himself like Jesus, suspending refugee programs, and almost allowing the livestream execution of a prisoner. And though he says the Bible is his favorite book, it’s hard to believe he can stomach a narrative that elevates another power above his own. The lack of pictures probably doesn’t help, either.

Regardless, white evangelicals continue to approve of Trump and his political juggernaut in shockingly high numbers, albeit less resoundingly than they did last year. But across the country, Republican candidates replicating his cheap political playbook aren’t faring as well.

Nowhere is this more apparent, of course, than the messy Senate brawl in Texas.

In one corner, we have MAGA adherent Ken Paxton, perhaps the single most morally bankrupt Senate candidate in the country—and it’s generally a competitive category. A self-identified Christian, Paxton cannot name what church he attends.

In the other corner, Talarico—a theologian, oratorical talent, and former underdog in this race—has embraced the campaign slogan “It’s time to start flipping tables,” a direct reference to the passage in the Bible when Jesus admonished merchants for corrupting a sacred temple with exploitative commerce. It’s David and Goliath if Goliath were indicted on two counts of securities fraud.

But Talarico isn’t the only Democrat closing the “God gap.” Senator (and Reverend) Raphael Warnock set the stage with his Baptist pride and 2021 Senate win—and he’s not ruling out a 2028 run for the presidency. And at least six Democrats running for office this cycle are ordained clergy, including Kansas’s Adam Hamilton, who, with the support of prominent local Republicans, has turned his deep-red state into a battleground.

It’s not just Christians, either. Mayor Zohran Mamdani openly celebrates his Muslim faith, despite Islamophobic backlash. And Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed continues to embrace his Muslim identity ahead of his contentious election in Michigan. Their example is broadening the definition of what a “faith-first candidate” means in America.

And in turning toward faith, Democrats are far from alone. After years in slow free fall, the share of Americans who identify as Christian is no longer declining. Meanwhile, 31 percent of Americans now see religion as gaining influence—still a distinct minority, but that’s the highest number Pew has measured in 15 years.

Perhaps, with everyday life increasingly filled with misinformation, AI deepfakes, and broad losses in institutional confidence, more Americans are seeking comfort beyond empiricism. It’s no surprise, then, that Gen Z, facing the host of problems we’ve left them with, might be more religious than other generations.

By long ceding the pulpit to Republicans, liberals only made it easier for the right to smuggle cruel policies and ugly bigotries into our political mainstream under the guise of religion. With this new crop of faith-fluent Democrats, however, the left may have found a potent way to fight back. After all, as Talarico has said, quoting scripture, “You can’t love God and hate other people.”

For decades, Republicans have dominated the intersection of religion and American politics. Now Democrats like James Talarico and Raphael Warnock are drawing on their faith to articulate a different vision of public life.

Texas Senate candidate James Talarico is invoking Christian teachings to challenge Republican policies on immigration, healthcare, and poverty. His campaign reflects a broader effort by religious Democrats to reclaim the language of faith.

From Christian clergy running for Congress to Muslim politicians embracing their religious identities, a new generation of Democratic candidates is challenging the assumption that faith-based politics belongs exclusively to the right.

Cohen) of Voices of Glasnost: Interviews with Gorbachev’s Reformers.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Even Republicans Are Waking Up to Trump’s Corruption
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Donald Trump walks on the south lawn of the White House on October 18, 2026.

Donald Trump’s near-total ability to get away with unprecedented corruption has always been one of the most frustrating aspects of his time atop US politics. Trump has been far and away the most crooked president in American history, a genuine gangster who makes earlier criminal presidents such as Warren Harding and Richard Nixon look like small-time hoodlums. His corruption extended from his brazen disdain for the Emoluments Clause in his first term (which allowed him to pocket millions of dollars from political supplicants trying to influence him by paying to stay at his hotels) to his family’s grand-scale self-enrichment in his second term (mostly through business deals in crypto and real estate, which have ballooned the Trump clan’s net worth by billions).

Yet Trump has paid virtually no price for this record-breaking larceny. Neither of his impeachments stemmed from his love of graft; the first involved political misconduct and the second from his incitement of the January 6 insurrection. And congressional Democrats, with a few notable exceptions such as Senator Elizabeth Warren, have been reluctant to challenge Trump on his personal corruption.

The political logic behind this reluctance to make corruption a political issue went something like this: Trump has a cult-like hold over the Republican electorate, so there is no convincing his voters that he is enriching himself. Further, voters care more about their own economic well-being than about what the Trump family is up to, while Republican elites are attuned to foreign-policy issues and threats to the constitutional order. Based on this reasoning, Democrats pursued a dual strategy of talking about economic issues to the electorate while trying to win over congressional Republicans on impeachments focused on Russiagate or Trump’s attempted coup.

My Nation colleague Chris Lehmann has repeatedly hammered the Democratic Party’s political elite for its aversion to making corruption a political issue. On my podcast, The Time of Monsters, last June, Lehmann rightly lamented the mental blinkers of thinking that kitchen-table economics and Trump’s corruption are separate issues. During the Watergate scandal, popular anger at Nixon’s slush fund intensified because of the concurrent rise in inflation. Under Trump, one could easily harness rage at the affordability crisis by contrasting the struggles of everyday voters with the orgy of self-enrichment in the White House, indulged in by both the president and his plutocratic cronies. David Sirota of The Lever has often made similar arguments about the necessity of foregrounding an anti-corruption message.

The good news is that Trump’s invulnerability on corruption seems to be ending. Two crucial groups are starting to wake up to the danger of a mobster president: a rising minority of Republican voters and many Democratic Party political consultants.

Nearly 2 in 3 Americans say President Donald Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself—and most of the increase over the past year has come from people who lean Republican, according to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll.

Among Republicans and independents who lean Republican, 34 percent believe Trump is enriching himself, up from 22 percent in September 2025. Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents were already nearly unanimous, at 88 percent a year ago and 92 percent now, while independents who don’t lean toward either party were unchanged.

Another striking fact is that in this poll, the percentage of independents who believe Trump is corrupt remained steady at a very high level: 72 percent.

Further, a Fox News poll released last Wednesday made clear that corruption was a top concern for a supermajority of voters. Asked what issues they were concerned with, corruption came out on top, with 88 percent concerned, including 60 percent saying they were extremely concerned. Intriguingly, the other issues that voters are worried about are economic. As Fox reports, “The top five voter concerns are government corruption (60% extremely concerned), inflation (58%), gas prices (50%), government leadership (49%), and healthcare (48%). And double digits more trust the Democrats than the Republicans to handle each of those.”

These polls (and other earlier ones) vindicate the argument long made by writers such as Lehmann and Sirota: Democrats need to hammer the Trump administration on corruption and link that with broader frustration about the economy.

On October 10, Politico reported that Democrats are “leaning hard into anti-corruption messaging in the final weeks of the campaign as new research suggests that linking corruption to Americans’ economic struggles can boost Democrats into the home stretch.” Josh Turek, the Democratic Senate candidate in Iowa, summed up the new argument succinctly: “We have a corruption crisis in this country, and it is leading to an affordability crisis.”

Similar arguments are being sounded by other Senate candidates, notably Jon Ossoff in Georgia, James Talarico in Texas, and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. According to Talarico, “We have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis.” Speaking at a rally on Saturday, Ossoff thundered, “The Mar-a-Lago mafia really has taken American corruption to spectacular new heights. This corruption is why nothing works for ordinary people.”

The new focus on corruption as an economic issue is welcome, but it is also just a start. While Trump’s grandiose personal corruption offers a massive target, it is merely a symptom of the larger problem of the plutocracy that has swallowed up so much of American politics. Beyond the midterms, anti-corruption politics can win only if Democrats deliver on the promise of reining in the oligarchs and giving ordinary people a bigger share of the economic pie. A failure to deliver on economic populism will only prepare the groundwork for another Trump-style demagogue.

Jeet Heer is a national affairs correspondent for The Nation and host of the weekly Nation podcast, The Time of Monsters. He also pens the monthly column “Morbid Symptoms.” The author of In Love with Art: Francoise Mouly’s Adventures in Comics with Art Spiegelman (2013) and Sweet Lechery: Reviews, Essays and Profiles (2014), Heer has written for numerous publications, including The New Yorker, The Paris Review, Virginia Quarterly Review, The American Prospect, The Guardian, The New Republic, and The Boston Globe.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Mamdani Can No Longer Avoid the Issue of the NYPD
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The mayor has been able to put difficult questions about policing on the back burner—until now.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch arrive to attend the New York City Police Department Memorial Wall on October 13, 2026.

Zohran Mamdani’s first year in Gracie Mansion has—unusually for a New York City mayor—mostly been an unquestionable PR success. Thanks to tangible quality-of-life improvements, some early wins on his agenda, and Mamdani’s world-class communications skills, his constituents actually seem to like him.

But no elected official can avoid rough patches forever. The bill always comes due. And, in New York City, that bill often comes attached to perhaps the single most powerful, divisive entity in the five boroughs: the New York City Police Department.

Mamdani, both during his mayoral campaign and now in office, has tried, and mostly succeeded, in reaching a broad truce with the NYPD without alienating a leftist base restless to rein it in. Movement advocates have so far given him grace on his reluctance to deliver on their demands for police reform, which largely predate Mamdani’s time in office. But in recent weeks, events have pushed that uneasy peace to a breaking point, brought the NYPD to the forefront of the political conversation, and underscored the challenges and contradictions inherent in moving from socialist outsider to the executive of the largest city in America.

First, there was the backlash following a protest outside the United Nations against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu—a man Mamdani thinks should be sent to The Hague. The NYPD arrested dozens of protesters, including some elected officials who, like Mamdani, are members of the Democratic Socialists of America. Some of the police officers were members of the Strategic Response Group, an NYPD unit ostensibly founded as a counterterrorism force but that mostly functions to arrest and brutalize protesters. Mamdani has vowed to abolish the SRG, but has yet to follow through on his promise.

That controversy was followed by an even bigger one over the horrific ICE shooting of 28-year-old Oscar Belgal in the Marble Hill neighborhood last week. The presence of ICE in the city, along with scenes of NYPD officers roughing up protesters who had mobilized in the wake of the shooting—including DSA-affiliated congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier—pushed the dissatisfaction of the left to new heights.

The national leadership of DSA called on Mamdani to abolish both the SRG and the Community Response Team, an anti-crime unit formed during Eric Adams’s tenure that has a pattern of brutalizing New Yorkers. And, most contentiously, DSA demanded that Mamdani fire NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch, the conservative billionaire heiress who was appointed by Adams and whose approach to policing would be familiar to anyone who lived under Rudy Giuliani’s “broken windows” regime. (The New York City chapter of DSA was more circumspect, saying that Mamdani should fire Tisch if she did not “end NYPD complicity with ICE and ensure that the NYPD is not used as a weapon against New Yorkers exercising their right to free speech, or as a shield for ICE’s unchecked violence.”)

Firing Tisch is not a new demand, nor one restricted to the socialist left; nonprofits like the NYCLU were strongly critical of her tenure long before Mamdani took office. This week, city councillors Julie Won and Carmen De La Rosa—neither of whom identify as socialists or are affiliated with DSA—called on the mayor to replace Tisch. But the controversy around Tisch’s presence in the role had mostly lain dormant until the past few weeks.

When asked by a reporter at a press conference this week if he would be open to replacing the police commissioner, Mamdani reiterated that he would be keeping Tisch where she was, and went on to praise her record of “uprooting corruption” and “lowering crime across our city.”

So where does all this leave Mamdani, the city’s left, and, most crucially, the prospects for reform of the NYPD?

Mamdani largely shied away from debates on crime and public safety on the campaign trail and was clear that he would not run on defunding the NYPD, but he ran on a public-safety platform that was at the very least interested in curbing the agency’s most egregious excesses and creating more humane civilian alternatives to police in addressing issues like homelessness. He promised to abolish the SRG and get rid of the NYPD’s controversial gang database, which unconstitutionally surveilled tens of thousands of Black and Latino New Yorkers.

Thus far, he has mostly not delivered on those promises, and even walked some of them back; just a few days after his swearing-in, Mamdani stood with Commissioner Tisch at a January 6 press conference as she praised the gang database for helping deliver the safest year in New York’s recorded history. According to testimony from Public Advocate Jumaane Williams in front of the New York City Council Committee on Public Safety, individuals could end up in the database for actions as mundane as “wishing a gang member a happy birthday on social media, being outside late and wearing a certain color, and living in the same public housing complex as accused gang members.” At a press conference in April, Mamdani signaled his intent to reform rather than abolish the database, noting that the NYPD “has also implemented a number of reforms as per the recommendation that came through.”

And he has set up a clear dividing line between his administration and some of his base by rejecting the calls to oust Tisch. That is not necessarily because he fears backlash from within the NYPD. The police unions are hostile to anything they perceive as reform measures, but keeping Tisch should be seen more as a bid to manage elite perception than an effort to keep the NYPD in line. While Tisch has spent much of her public-sector career at the NYPD, she is not exactly a creature of the department. Unusually for a police commissioner, she has never actually served as a police officer, holding a variety of civilian positions in the department, and has since held other executive positions in city government across multiple administrations. Less than two years ago, she was Adams’s sanitation commissioner, and said publicly many times that the position was her “dream job.”

Tisch’s value proposition to Mamdani is that she is well-connected. A daughter of one of the wealthiest families in New York City and a personal friend of Ivanka Trump, she is well-regarded among New York’s elite. Governor Kathy Hochul advocated for keeping Tisch on as police commissioner behind the scenes in 2025, and has gone on the record praising Mamdani for “bringing in real pros.” Both Hochul and House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries cited his keeping Tisch on as a factor in their decision to endorse Mamdani in the general election last year.

So far, Mamdani has shown a willingness to engage with some of the movement’s demands, and this week he indicated future action on the SRG. Whether that means he will abolish the unit or simply reform it remains to be seen. But there is no indication that, even if the SRG were to disappear, other NYPD units would not simply adopt its anti-protest functions—as well as its aggressive and sometimes unconstitutional methods. Abolishing the SRG would also set up a direct clash with Tisch, who supports maintaining the unit.

Tisch’s remaining in her position embodies some of the inherent dissonance of a democratic socialist’s being the chief executive of New York City, overseeing a police force of over 33,000 officers. The mayor comes from activist spaces, but is now at the heart of the political establishment. His campaign appealed to New Yorkers interested in a vision for city government that put them, not the ultra-wealthy, first, but a politician in a city as large and complicated as New York has to navigate the often competing demands of lots of different groups, not just that of his base. He is a supporter of Palestinian liberation whose police commissioner, a self-described “proud Zionist,” apologized to a synagogue hosting an illegal land sale that was the target of pro-Palestine protesters. He has made concrete promises around policing, but is also eager not to become a target of the NYPD’s ire, as confrontation with the police unions or the threat of a police strike could derail his administration.

These contradictions inevitably force someone in Mamdani’s situation to make divisive choices, like the choice he has now made to keep Tisch. There are many who see that as a politically sensible way for the mayor to maintain momentum on the other key parts of his agenda for the benefit of the working class without getting drawn into the NYPD quicksand. But there are others who will see this as a sign that New York’s wealthiest are still calling the shots on public safety—and that fundamental police reform remains as out of reach as ever. It’s too early to see how all of this will play out. But one thing seems certain: The days of Zohran Mamdani’s being able to avoid the NYPD-shaped elephant in the room are over.

https://theintercept.com/2026/10/20/kohe.title: Kohen Wiley’s Family Say They Never Heard From Investigators Who Concluded Cops Did No Wrong
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/20/kohe.text:
For months, the residents of Senatobia, Mississippi, have waited with a mix of dread and anticipation for state authorities to decide what, if anything, they plan to do about the killing of Kohen Wiley. Ever since the 1-year-old child was shot by a white police officer outside a local Walmart in June, organizers have held protests and press conferences outside the town’s city hall, to call for accountability — or even a simple acknowledgment — for the loss of the Black toddler.

On Monday, Senatobia residents got their answer: Officials plan to do nothing. “In this incident, the Attorney General’s Office found the use of force was justified,” Republican Mississippi AG Lynn Fitch announced in a three-sentence news release posted on her official website.

The announcement was met with anguish and outrage from people inside and outside the state. The Mississippi Legislative Black Caucus demanded further answers. “Kohen Wiley was a baby,” said state Rep. Kabir Karriem, who chairs the MLBC. “He posed no threat. He deserved protection, and he deserved a future. His family is owed more than a conclusion. … Announcing that a review is complete does not fulfill the responsibility to explain how a police encounter ended with a baby dead.”

The attorney general’s decision followed a probe into the case by the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, which was “responsible for conducting a thorough and impartial investigation,” as Mississippi Department of Public Safety Press Secretary Alex Gibert wrote to The Intercept on Tuesday. The email said that the probe “remains open and active.” But in a subsequent phone call, Gibert said that the investigation “involving the officer is closed.”

Gibert reiterated what the agency has previously said: that body camera footage and other investigative materials will be made available through public records requests. But she added that nothing will be released until after officials meet with Wiley’s family. “We are meeting with the family later this week,” she said.

As recently as Monday, however, the family maintained they had received no communication from the state. Kohen’s grandmother, Veronica Roberson, told Mississippi Today that she found out about the attorney general’s decision on Facebook and that no one had reached out. The outlet also reported last month that, although the investigation was complete and on the attorney general’s desk as of mid-September, no one had interviewed Kohen’s mother, Vel’lesiya Wiley, who was holding her child in her lap when he was shot dead by police. This called into question whether the investigation is as “thorough” as authorities have claimed. Asked by The Intercept whether the MBI investigation sought to interview Wiley, Gibert said she could not comment.

The man who killed Baby Kohen, as the child is now known, was identified by the press as Senatobia Police Sgt. Hunter Foster, who fired his gun into the car where Wiley was riding in the passenger’s seat on June 14. The exact circumstances that led to the shooting remain murky. Police said that officers responded to a shoplifting call at the Walmart; a two-page incident log released to The Intercept via a public records request contained no information about the shooting but noted that the items allegedly stolen were baby clothes and a pack of Pampers.

In a video posted on social media shortly after her child was killed, Wiley said she got into the passenger’s seat of the Ford Fusion after the driver, Latoya Ferrell, was stopped on her way out of the store. Police accused the women of trying to flee; according to Wiley, when she saw officers approach with guns drawn, she said, “I raised my baby up” to warn that he was in the car. Then the police shot him. Ferrell was also struck and was hospitalized, but survived.

Most Read Inside ICE, Officials Question String of Trump Admin “Midterm Panic Moves” Karl Loftus Lockheed Martin Showered Susan Collins With Cash as F-35 Program Hit Turbulence Noah Hurowitz Dems Have an Opportunity to Force an End to the Iran War. Will They Take It? Matt Sledge

The Senatobia Police Department immediately claimed that the car drove toward police, almost hitting them — an account swiftly echoed by the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation. But to date, officials have released no evidence to support this account. Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who took the family’s case, hired an outside pathologist to do an external examination of the child and to review visual evidence. In July, the medical examiner concluded, based on the appearance of the injuries and path of the fatal bullet, that the officer shot the baby from the side of the car, undermining the police’s version of events.

The announcement by the attorney general has renewed long-standing calls for video to be released. In a press conference held earlier this month, local activist Patrick Lumumba of the Senatobia Committee for Accountability and Transparency accused the state of tailoring its investigation to support a lie — that Wiley and Ferrell deliberately sought to strike Foster with the car.

“If video footage would prove that, they would have released it the next day,” he said.

The killing of Kohen Wiley drew national attention to Senatobia, a small city just south of Memphis, Tennessee. City leaders mostly refused to address the killing, save for a brief, scripted video released by Senatobia Mayor Greg Graves a few days after the shooting. By the time Kohen’s family laid him to rest in late June, the police narrative had prompted many inside and outside Senatobia to blame Kohen’s mother for his death, with rumors suggesting that, rather than charge the police officer, authorities would charge the mother and driver.

The child’s death followed years of warnings by Black residents over the police’s treatment of adults and children alike. Among the string of high-profile incidents was the jailing of a 10-year-old boy for public urination, as well as the violent arrest of two sisters, 13 and 14, outside a public housing complex. According to the girls and their mother, then-police chief Richard Chandler personally ordered one of the girls to “get your Black ass out of the road” before forcing her to the ground. And on Mother’s Day 2025 — in the same Walmart parking lot where Kohen Wiley would be shot dead — a female officer forced a woman out of her car in front of her young children for sitting in a handicapped parking space.

In the summer of 2025, the Senatobia Board of Aldermen dismissed Chandler, replacing him with interim police chief Harold Vanderford, a move aimed at restoring trust, as one alderman put it. But the killing of Kohen Wiley revealed that, in reality, nothing had changed.

Residents of Senatobia, including one former law enforcement officer, told The Intercept that the institutional culture brought by Chandler remained entrenched, with Senatobia officers showing disdain and disregard for the community. City records also showed that the chief had pushed the city to adopt new ordinances that would bring in revenue for the police department, while expanding punishments for misdemeanors like loitering.

At several board of alderman meetings over the summer, Lumumba and other activists reminded city leaders that they’d warned officials about the danger posed to Black residents by Senatobia police. At the same time, Mississippi Today revealed evidence that Foster had a history of racist remarks. Just days before he shot Kohen Wiley, Foster was accused of making racist comments to a Black colleague, who later left the police department. Foster is still on the force, on paid leave.

Then, in late August, Mississippi Today exposed racist text messages sent by Vanderford himself. The text messages dated back to the summer of 2025 and contained more than a dozen uses of the N-word. City leadership initially tried to sweep the scandal under the rug: Vanderford claimed that the messages were created by AI and, after a closed-door meeting, the mayor and members of Senatobia’s board of aldermen announced that Vanderford would stay on. But individual aldermen pushed back publicly. On September 1, Vanderford tried to resign, only for the board to announce that they had voted to fire him. Vanderford was replaced by a Black woman, Senatobia Police Lieutenant Angelica Maze.

In a statement accepting the appointment as interim chief on September 5, Maze did what the police department had previously failed to do: express “heartfelt condolences to Kohen Wiley’s family and to everyone in the community who has been affected by this tragic loss.”

In another statement on Monday, after the attorney general announced the use of force was justified, Maze acknowledged that the community “may have questions, concerns, and strong emotions, and we respect everyone’s right to express their views peacefully.”

With the body camera footage likely to be released within the next several days, a new round of waiting begins in Senatobia. In the meantime, the Senatobia Committee for Accountability and Transparency released a statement on social media.

“This was never just a news story for us. It was personal – many of us are residents of Senatobia and parents of vulnerable children. … We are also human beings who need time to grieve, reflect, and process everything that has transpired.”

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

I’M BEN MUESSIG, The Intercept’s editor-in-chief. It’s been a devastating year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.title: The Genius of Charli XCX
https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.text:
The last time a Charli XCX album appeared—her sixth studio album, by the evocative title of Brat—the Club was ascendant. By that, I mean not a specific club but that quasi-mythological space, known to humankind for at least a century, where you dance away your emotional burdens into the wee hours of the morning. Here, as a Russian clubgoer once famously observed, “The ladies look good, the alcohol is flowing. There is much pain in the world, but not in this room.” That summer, in the not-so-distant year of 2024, Kamala Harris was projected to win the upcoming presidential election, fans and marketers declared Charli’s album to be the sound of the season, and “Brat Summer” was born, screaming, into a world that promised to be a little less chaotic.

Of course, we know how 2024 ended. Two years later, at the end of another record-breaking summer, Charli has given us something new: Music, Fashion, Film, an album whose title seems to gesture toward carefree living. But that would be too easy, I think. The album appears in the second year of another interminable Trump presidency, full of the nothing-signifying sound and fury that his return to office has wrought, and it sounds nothing like its predecessor. Of course, our sociopolitical vibes are different these days as well.

But, thank God, so is the music. Despite featuring a couple of the same producers who appeared on Brat—A.G. Cook and Finn Keane—the album is vastly different: It sounds, in a word, like rock. Its title also hints at something else: Charli’s renewed focus on her creative ventures outside of music. In addition to being the Club’s princess, she’s one of the faces of Saint Laurent and an actress appearing in more and more independent films. That Charli is less well-known in these domains appears to have given her some productive creative anxiety, pushing her music in new directions in the process. “I think the dance floor is dead / So now we’re making rock music,” she sings in the title track. And the rest of the album lives up to that promise.

As an artist, Charli XCX has always been great at making meaning out of the prevailing cultural currents: Brat Summer only happened because the public finally caught up with her. Which is what is fascinating about a track like “SS26,” one of Music, Fashion, Film’s singles and among the best songs on the album. Here’s the chorus, which finds Charli dispensing a terminal diagnosis for an uncertain world:

﻿Spring, Summer ’26When the world is gonna end, no hope for any of itYeah, we’re walkin’ on a runway that goes straight to hellNothing’s gonna save us, not music, fashion, or film.

It’s unusually straightforward songwriting, and it’s not hard to feel that Charli is correct once again: As governments around the world continue their inexorable rightward slide; as Europe, Canada, and the western United States are consumed by intense wildfires; as the American president continues to send fuel prices spiraling globally, it’s getting harder to deny that hell is real and that, as a great writer once said, it is other people.

But with that last line in mind (“Nothing’s gonna save us, not music, fashion, or film”), it is, I think, easier to read the thrust of the new album: that our outlets of escape can’t save us. A little later in the song, Charli has some even sharper words for the culture. “Think my politics could work as a press strategy / And my heritage could give me quite the USP [unique selling point, in marketing-speak] / Can’t hide the fact that I’d rather take the easy road,” she sings. Me too, girl. If escaping into art is no longer enough, what is? Charli doesn’t give an answer for the rest of us, but she does provide one for herself, the last line of the verse: “Yeah, I think I’ll be all right if I look good in the clothes.” Obviously, she doesn’t believe it. But sung as sweetly as it is, over a pop-punkish bass line, a digital snare hit, and a tastefully minimal guitar, the song goes down easy.

Music, Fashion, Film gets darker as it goes on. To a set of grunge-y guitars that could come straight from a late-aughts alt-rock album, backed by MPC﻿-style digital beats, Charli gives us songs about her bedroom-pop-star days (“2007”), about how she can buy everything but a new life (“Card Declined”), and about her fear of ruining the best relationship in her life because of her own bad self (“I’m Afraid”). That’s a lot of self-disclosure, and in other hands it might feel maudlin—too vulnerable, too eager—but here the feelings are finely worked. It’s emotional vulnerability as a necessity, not as a marketing strategy (though it could be that too, of course).

“Do I wanna make music?” Charli asks in the middle of “Camera,” a song that’s largely about contemplating a career change. “Am I being fuckin’ stupid / If I try to be a girl on the screen when I’m turning thirty-four? / But all I know is how it makes me feel.” It’s refreshingly honest; she’s a narrator you can trust.

Still, the music’s fun, and I’m a sucker for depressing lyrics set to fun music. The tunes are spare in places, with seemingly simple instrumentation—but you can tell that a lot of thought went into the arrangements. Cook and Keane do a lot with what feels like a little, and it’s magic. Another notable thing: Charli sings without AutoTune, in a voice that’s minimally processed. It’s another sign that she’s moving forward.

Plus these songs have an outsize life and energy to them. Music, Fashion, Film isn’t all interiority: “2007” is a romp through the past, a reminder of how much fun it was to make music in your bedroom before the fame set in. “Magic Metal Montana,” on the other hand, swaps bouncy lyrics for poignant ones, as it’s a song to her friend and collaborator A.G. Cook. Its sweetest moment comes when she says, “I think you taught me, I think I taught you / You believe me, I believe you”—an expression of trust you don’t find in most love songs. And “Rock Music” is a fun night out with friends, with everyone having a good time as they feel their way through the moment.

If there’s a thesis statement on Music, Fashion, Film, it’s probably “No One Lasts Forever,” which is a reminder from Charli—to herself, to the world—that no matter what happens, no matter how much things change, no state of affairs can last forever, and none of us do either. The song is billed as “featuring David Cronenberg” because it has an extended snippet from an interview that she did with the famous body-horror director about a near-death experience he had; it’s the only featured appearance on the album.

“As I was lying there on the sidewalk,” Cronenberg says, “I did not think about art at all. I—I thought about people, I thought about life…. No, I was not thinking about art as endurance, as immortality. We can talk about immortal artists, and it can turn out that, yes, some artists have created art that has really survived thousands of years…. And that’s fantastic. But experientially, for them, they are dead, they are gone, they are not experiencing that…. I really feel, and hear me assuring you, that oblivion is freedom.”

It’s a funny lesson to throw in at the end of what is ostensibly a pop album, but somehow it works. Oblivion is freedom, yes—from obligation, from the pressures of fame, from everything annoying that we can’t change but that nevertheless makes us who we are. The Club is dead—Charli says so herself. Perhaps it’s time to accept the things we can’t escape, about our lives and about ourselves. Perhaps it’s time to chart a new way forward.

Bijan Stephen is a music critic for The Nation. He lives in New York and his other work has appeared in The New Yorker, The New Republic, Esquire, and elsewhere.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Why Democratic Leaders Keep Waging War on the Young
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The party’s silver-haired establishment is caught up in an existential culture war.

Because reactionaries are always with us, every age has its unique assortment of moral panics, both serious and benign. As a late Gen Xer, I faced plenty of eager efforts to pathologize my unforgivable youth, including the failed War on Drugs, inquisitions into the scourge of video games and MTV, which were plainly rotting the brains of children, and a crusade to reverse the alleged epidemic of teen pregnancy. And because I grew up Southern Baptist in Alabama, I also contended with menacing subgenres of these panics. Rooted in religious strictures against secularism, they rhymed with what was happening in the culture at large if you were seeing it narrowly though a pinhole. At the time and place I grew up, I witnessed how culture warriors viewed Salman Rushdie’s novel The Satanic Verses (which they’d obviously never read) as a handbook of occult practices, repudiated the Catholic artist Andres Serrano’s Piss Christ as blasphemous, and reprised rumors from the 1960s suggesting that if you played certain rock songs backwards, demons would talk to you—only this time via cassette tape instead of vinyl.

This vivid array of scares and campfire stories had one key through line: an ostensible concern with the horrors that an amoral and predatory culture were wreaking on the youth of America. There was a far-from-complicated animus at the heart of these complaints, particularly when our Boomer elders were wielding them: A generation that had been thrust onto the center stage of mid-century consumer capitalism was now seething with resentment that a successor demographic was storming the leading edge of culture via art, changing social norms, and especially politics, which, as the right-wing Gen Xer Andrew Breitbart famously argued, is always downstream from culture.

It’s hard to avoid viewing the current generational fractures within the Democratic Party through this lens. Where older Democrats differ from much younger ones, it’s generally along the lines of attitudes toward sexuality and gender and trust in institutions and authority figures (especially the police, the military, and religious and business leaders). These positions on culture and character in public life also readily translate into differing views on the role of government in society and the role of the United States in global affairs.

Nowhere are these fractures more apparent than in the growing, well-chronicled divide between the centrist and progressive wings of the party, the latter of which skews younger. So we’re not quibbling about definitions here, I’m going to use the Pew Research Center’s terminology for the two poles of the liberal coalition: The “leftward progressives” are the farthest left (and the youngest), while the members of the “order and opportunity left” are the farthest right.

Leftward progressives support trans rights and think billionaires are bad for society. They care about US involvement in global affairs but believe we mostly tend to make things worse. The members of the order-and-opportunity left are concerned about safety and are “moderate” on issues of sexuality and gender. This is a nice way of saying they’re happy with some immigration restrictions, generally trust law enforcement, think gender is mostly determined by sex assigned at birth, and tend to whine if anyone asks about their pronouns.

Leftward progressives overwhelmingly vote Democratic (97 percent went for Kamala Harris in 2024) but express some dissatisfaction with the party. In a survey published in 2026, Pew found a clear correlation between higher age and lower progressive sentiment within the party, with leftward progressives accounting for 26 percent of Democrats and Democratic leaners under 30 and 15 percent in the 30-to-49 cohort. From there, the drop-off is steep: Leftward progressives make up just 6 percent of the Democratic-aligned 50-and-older group. Not surprisingly, the picture for the order-and-opportunity left is a virtual photographic negative, comprising 15 percent of Democratic and Democratic-leaning voters under 30, 22 percent of those in the 30-to-49 cohort, and 31 percent of those in the 50-and-older group.

These categories are not perfect, but they still give a strong account of the generational disparities in voter attitudes. They are decent proxies for the younger, more progressive left and the older, more centrist liberals. The issues these two groups disagree on constitute the fault line that runs through the Democratic Party right now, presenting real challenges for a party that’s long been assailed as a stodgy gerontocracy—and, tellingly, the ascribed responsibility for this growing schism tends to increase as one moves down the life-cycle chart. According to much of the discourse coming from Democratic officialdom, the problem—as always—is kids these days.

The leftward progressives align closely in spirit and demography with the Democratic Socialists of America. Despite its relatively small national membership (in the low six figures), the DSA is a ready stand-in for the wide-ranging establishment lamentations about leftist overreach. The DSA’s status as the de facto brand for a political youth movement is not incidental to the critique; it’s a load-bearing wall.

And the DSA has gotten younger over the past decade. In 2013, the average age of a DSA member was 67. After Donald Trump was elected in 2016, it was 33—a trend that, like the overall growth of the organization, largely stems from the insurgent presidential candidacies of the outlying progressive octogenarian Bernie Sanders. Thirty-three isn’t that young, but given the median age of a member of Congress (57.5 in the House and 64.7 in the Senate as of January 2025), DSA members are practically tweens.

The fact that younger members of the DSA—the people most responsible for having increased the national membership so quickly, from 5,000 just before Trump’s first election to more than 120,000 today—are playing a more prominent role, as well as leadership fights within the organization, have led to some generational fractures even in the DSA itself, particularly over the issue of Israel’s genocide in Gaza. Maurice Isserman, who had been a member of the DSA for over 40 years, wrote in The Nation in 2023 about quitting the organization, claiming that it had become too harsh in its broadsides against Israel and wasn’t criticizing Hamas harshly enough. At its core, this is a rehash of the old antisemitism argument: that a particular concern for Palestinian lives is effectively a pointed attack on Jewish ones. Isserman cited “the singularly important role of Palestine in DSA’s rather short list of international concerns, completely overshadowing the attention paid, for example, to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, or to the rights of other oppressed peoples, like the Kurdish Muslims, or China’s Uyghur Muslims.”

This has become a common refrain among older Democrats: that the situation in Gaza is of interest to young people only because it allows them to criticize Israel and, by extension, Jews. (This argument relies on a disingenuous and dangerous conflation of Israeli nationalism and Judaism that’s been weaponized by the right, but that is a sermon for another time.) It’s telling that Isserman elides the very obvious reason why younger progressives might be more vocal about the Gaza genocide: The United States has provided more economic and military aid to Israel than any other country since the founding of the Israeli state—an outlay of at least $21.7 billion since October 7 alone. We (and here “we” includes DSA members, who pay taxes just like the rest of the Democratic coalition) are not providing billions in aid to Russia, China, or the persecutors of Kurdish Muslims in Syria or Iran.

This posture, in other words, isn’t a consequence of undue hostility toward Israel so much as it’s a reflection of moral injury: the feeling that something must be done, but that structural forces block effective moral action. Older generations remember a very different set of attitudes toward Israel, and many assume that the relationship is or should remain the same as it has always been. Younger generations are more likely to view the US–Israeli relationship through the lens of Netanyahu’s regime and its attendant barbarisms, which they have more direct evidence of thanks to social media and a 24/7 news cycle. Of course they feel more strongly about it than conflicts in which the United States is either ostensibly on the right side (as in Russia’s war with Ukraine) or has far less involvement.

But that doesn’t stop high-profile centrists from insisting that anyone below a certain age who is critical of Israel’s actions in Gaza is antisemitic, especially if they happen to be a brown person. Case in point: The Atlantic’s Jonathan Chait, who wrote a column about Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed’s relationship with Hasan Piker, whom Chait deems antisemitic for noting that it’s dangerous to conflate Israel and Judaism—a point echoed by many other Jewish people in the political center.

This brings us to another divide between the older generation and the younger: technology. If you don’t know who Hasan Piker is, he’s a political streamer on social media whose views are progressive. He is not the left’s Joe Rogan, because Rogan has said many more offensive things and no one is telling Republicans or California Governor Gavin Newsom to disassociate themselves from him. Nor is Piker formally connected to the Democratic Party apparatus. But he is popular with the youth. He has 3.1 million followers on Twitch and 1.9 million on YouTube. This level of influence is largely why centrist Democrats have determined that he is not just a problem but a “crisis,” in Chait’s alarmist formulation.

Determined to outdo Chait, the Democratic strategist James Carville has threatened to leave the Democratic Party entirely if Piker (who, again, is not a candidate, an operative, a consultant, or an officer of the DNC) becomes more of a “force.” “I am not going to be in the same party with Hasan Piker,” Carville proclaimed during one performance in his endless regress of kids-these-days cable hits.

Such tantrum-throwing may play well on television, but it makes for terrible political judgment. The ’90s-bred cult of studious difference-trimming and capitulation to the right that Carville helped pioneer continues to reinforce the Democrats’ image as a party terminally dedicated to preserving the status quo. In one recent, all-too-typical case, Representative Hakeem Jeffries, who will likely be the next House speaker if the Democrats do well in the midterms, faced a massive backlash after he met with Jared Kushner to discuss ways the Democrats could work with the Trump administration. Jeffries is on the younger end of the establishment (he’s 56) but is politically synched with his mentor Nancy Pelosi and Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer.

Our seniority-heavy caste of democratic leaders have been slower to acknowledge that we are in extraordinary times. In 2019, I wrote about Pelosi’s reluctance to impeach Trump (she said he was self-impeaching) and her simultaneous bigfooting of the newly elected leftist congresswomen who made up “the Squad.” Pelosi came around on impeaching Trump, but she went on to block Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez from the senior position on the House Oversight Committee in favor of Gerry Connolly, a 74-year-old who died of cancer shortly after his appointment. Pelosi’s generation of leaders is quick to protect the management cohort of the party—which is now a full-on gerontocracy—from any encroachment by younger elected officials, even at the expense of the party’s future.

And they are incapable of acting as an opposition party; they don’t have the stomach for it. Their political instincts were formed during an era when elections were not determined, as they are now, almost entirely by negative partisanship. During the ’90s heyday of most of the figures who now make up the party’s leadership, engaging in civility theater was a sign of political maturity. Now voters view it mostly as a sign of weakness.

The former New York City comptroller and current Democratic nominee for Congress Brad Lander, a DSA-aligned progressive who jointly campaigned with Zohran Mamdani for mayor, has described the divide among Democrats as “folders” versus “fighters.” This line breaks down generationally, too. In this political environment, writing “very strong letters,” taking closed-door meetings with Trumpists, adopting Republican talking points about gender expression in the guise of “just asking questions,” and dismissing the concerns of women and people of color as “identity politics” looks like folding. Pushing for big systemic reforms that will trigger formidable political challenges (universal healthcare, tax reform that puts more of the burden on the rich and less on the poor, ambitious housing goals) looks like fighting. Standing up for trans people, criticizing the United States’ role in providing weapons to Israel, and biting back at GOP insults looks like fighting.

Younger Democrats are simply better equipped to act like an opposition party—in part because they don’t have the experience of being in power, either as a party or as an age cohort. They are less willing to wait patiently until the next election—or the next one or the next one—for Democrats to gain new seats or get around to exercising whatever power they already have.

I’m 49 years old and taught at New York University for six years and the School of Visual Arts for six years before that. I’ve worked on Democratic campaigns of all stripes, some with DSA candidates (including one with a younger Zohran Mamdani) and some with older, more moderate candidates in red states. I have been around many young Democrats; I’ve taught them, hired them, and also witnessed directly the pushback they get from Boomers and Gen Xers who resent their efforts to exert real political power instead of just sitting on the sidelines until they’re old and rich enough to own a house and have kids.

Yet the relevant divides remain as stubbornly cultural as they are material. It’s generally the case that older generations oppose student protests on the apparent assumption that students should earn their right to dissent, as if the First Amendment is something you graduate into.

When I defend younger activists and candidates, I always prepare for a barrage of facts about the alleged erratic levels of political engagement among this cohort that are technically true but often willfully misinterpreted. The first of these cherished data points is the one showing that younger people don’t vote as reliably as older people. But the people who cite this statistic assume it’s because the youths are too self-involved, or lazy, or possibly hungover from last night’s party. They almost never acknowledge that young people’s voter participation is heavily dictated by systems that fundamentally work against them.

Voting is a habit, and it’s instilled over many years as people get used to the cadence of elections—particularly in traditionally low-turnout contests such as primaries and downballot races. In addition, campaigns can’t afford to target everyone, so they often seek to identify likely supporters among those who have consistently voted over a period of years, which obviously leaves out younger people. Plus, the political participation of college students is actively suppressed by the right, which assumes that they’re more liberal than the general population. And it’s astonishingly easy to impose voter-suppression measures at universities and colleges where students are living away from home.

As a simple matter of self-preservation, elected officials (many of whom are much, much older if we’re talking about Congress) are less responsive to the needs of people who don’t have children or own homes. Younger voters are much less likely to fall within this charmed circle of the electorate than their grandparents—in part because of the political and economic windfalls that the older generation received.

Despite all of this, young people have been going to the polls in greater numbers over the past decade. As of this writing, the 35-year-old mayor of New York City is the seventh-most-popular Democrat in the country, and AOC is the fourth. Both are dues-paying members of the DSA.

Leftward progressivism, as Pew calls it, is not just a youth movement (plenty of us on the left are old!). But it is a youth movement culturally, even as it’s built on the work of earlier generations. Because of that, older elements in the Democratic coalition find it threatening; it marshals a political movement around changing social norms, concerns motivated by a sense of moral injury during a formative period of life, differing expectations about what government can and should do, and a justifiably righteous conviction that it’s better to fight and lose on hard issues than not to fight at all. Which makes it very much like virtually every youth movement that came before it.

The idea that progressive young people are sabotaging the party from within with pronouns, keffiyehs, and wild, irrational ideas about what the government should be able to do for people that governments in other developed countries routinely manage to do is just another moral panic. I expect that the younger members of the party who emerge as leaders will prove their elders wrong. You can indeed see this process unfolding right now in Mamdanistan, where we have less violent crime, faster pothole repairs, a handful of city-owned grocery stores slated to open, and no open revolts.

Elizabeth Spiers is a digital media strategist and writer living in Brooklyn. She is the former editor in chief of The New York Observer.

In a world dominated by neoliberal market fundamentalism, “socialism” is what will make a more moderate, regulated form of capitalism work for most people.
